questions.title: What is the physical intuition behind the Bradley-Terry cancellation in the derivation of Eq. (12)?
questions.question_body:
In Section 5, the paper derives the DPO objective by rearranging the optimal policy equation (Eq. 10) to isolate the reward $r(x,y)$ (Eq. 11), interpreting them as equivalent representations of a model being a 'secretly' reward model. Later, in Eq. 12), they substitute Eq. 11 into the Bradley-Terry preference formula (Eq. 5) and claim that the partition function $Z(x)$ 'cancels out,' resulting in a simple binary cross-entropy loss.

I understand mathematically how terms can cancel algebraically, but I am struggling to visualize *why* this works conceptually in this specific context of conditioning on $x$. If I have a dataset of pairs and labels, doesn't mathematically knowing that $r(x,y) = \beta \log [\frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}] + \beta \log Z(x)$ depend on $x$ break any simplification? Specifically, isn't $Z(x)$ a function of $x$ that varies between samples? What is preventing from seeing it como an unbiased estimate or value estimate that disappears during the subtraction?

questions.title: How can the gradient magnitude in Eq. (14) prevent generation degeneration if weight updates are only scaled by how 'wrong' the reward is?
questions.question_body:
The paper describes how gradients for DPO increase the likelihood of preferred completions while down-weighting gradient updates for dispreferred ones based on their implicit reward score (Eq. 14). It states that without this weighting term, naive updates lead to 'degeneration.'

However, I don't fully grasp *how* this weighting term acts as a regularizer against 'mode collapse' or 'reward hacking.' If the model just needs to satisfy enough preferences to converge, why would a uniform update cause it to collapse into a single high-reward token distribution? Is there an implicit inference about variance among reward estimates being necessary? Can you walk through exactly what happens step-by-step in an inner loop training step where this weighting plays a role?

questions.title: Why are DPO policies theoretically guaranteed to generalize better than PPO if they optimize identical objectives over different datasets?
questions.question_body:
The experiments section mentions that DPO performs well because it optimizes RLHF objectives but using only preference pairs, while PPO relies on ground-truth rewards and generates thousands of samples per forward pass.

I'm confused about why simply using fewer samples would theoretically improve generalization or reduce variance. While using fewer samples might seem intuitively faster, doesn't sampling multiple trajectories increase our variance estimates so that we can find better gradients? Can you explain why reducing our sample count actually leads to more robust policies or better utilities compared to increasing sample counts via generation?

questions.title: Why is Chef's initialization method for $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ described as equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation but different from standard supervised fine-tuning?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4 ('DPO outline'), the paper notes that when we do not have an SFT model available, we initialize our reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by fitting it directly on preferred responses using Maximum Likelihood Estimation:

$$ \pi_{\text{ref}} = \argmax_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{x, y_w \sim \mathcal{D}}[\log \pi(y_w \\mid x)] $$

My question centers: why shouldn't we just initialize $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ with this same MLE-trained model and proceed with DPO? Why does this specific setup require us to run Supervised Fine-Tuning first anyway? Is there some inherent bias or inconsistency with leaving two version of models separate before optimizations?

questions.title: 'Reward over-optimization' vs insufficiency: How does bias propagate when training only with preferred responses?
questions.question_body:
"Limitations & Future Work" section mentions:

> Additionally, while we evaluate models up to 6B parameters... whether reward over-optimization manifests in direct preference optimization setting... is clear decrease in perfomance an instance it?
What do you mean exactly by "reward over-optimization"?

In standard RLHF with PPO, over-optimization usually happens as you explode rewards without penalizing low probablities too harshly, leading you to discover many sequences which those reward labels give non-zero value. But here you did not train with reward for negative reinforcement at all; rather you forced negative outcomes so that positive ones get higher likelihoods.

I suspect there's some subtle connection between these — surely."Wantless patterns
